results.answer: Envoy attaches response flags to its access logs that pinpoint the exact failure reason: - `UF` = Upstream Connection Failure - `UC` = Upstream Connection Termination - `UO` = Upstream Overflow (circuit breaker tripped) - `NR` = No Route configured [istio_503_service_unavailable.md#istio_503_service_unavailable.md-c0] kubectl logs <client-pod> -c istio-proxy -n <namespace> | grep -E '503|UF|UC|UO|NR' [istio_503_service_unavailable.md#istio_503_service_unavailable.md-c2] [Check Envoy access logs for response flags] [istio_503_service_unavailable.md#istio_503_service_unavailable.md-c2]

results.question: How can legacy pods without an Istio sidecar connect to a STRICT mTLS service?
results.answer: When an Istio namespace or workload is configured with `PeerAuthentication` in `STRICT` mode, any client connecting over plain unencrypted TCP/HTTP without an authenticated mTLS certificate handshake will be immediately rejected with TCP connection reset or `connection termination`. [istio_mtls_strict_failures.md#istio_mtls_strict_failures.md-c0] By default, Istio will accept mTLS and non-mTLS traffic (often called "permissive mode"). Users can opt-in to strict enforcement by writing `PeerAuthentication` or `AuthorizationPolicy` rules requiring mTLS [index.md#index.md-c11] {{< text yaml >}} apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: PeerAuthentication metadata: name: default namespace: foo spec: mtls: mode: STRICT --- apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: AuthorizationPolicy metadata: name: foo-isolation namespace: foo spec: action: ALLOW rules: - from: - source: namespaces: ["foo"] {{< /text >}} [index.md#index.md-c3]

results.question: What Nginx ingress annotation should be tuned to resolve 504 Gateway Timeout on long-running APIs?
results.answer: HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout occurs when an edge proxy or Kubernetes Ingress Controller (Nginx Ingress, AWS Load Balancer Controller / ALB, Traefik) fails to receive a timely response from an upstream backend service pod within the configured timeout window [kubernetes_ingress_504_gateway_timeout.md#kubernetes_ingress_504_gateway_timeout.md-c0] Heavy database queries, slow external API calls, or garbage collection pauses exceed the default 60-second Nginx `proxy-read-timeout`. - **Immediate Fix:** Add timeout annotations to the Ingress resource: ```yaml metadata: annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-connect-timeout: "15" nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "180" nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "180" ``` For AWS ALB Ingress: ```yaml metadata: annotations: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-attributes: idle_timeout.timeout_seconds=180 [kubernetes_ingress_504_gateway_timeout.md#kubernetes_ingress_504_gateway_timeout.md-c6] Client sees:** `504 Gateway Time-out` - **Ingress Controller log shows:** `upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream` - **Impact:** Failed API transactions, degraded user checkout/request flows, and customer-facing incident alerts. [kubernetes_ingress_504_gateway_timeout.md#kubernetes_ingress_504_gateway_timeout.md-c0]

results.answer: When traffic arrives at an AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) or Network Load Balancer (NLB), target instances or container IPs in the Target Group fail health checks and are marked `Unhealthy`. - **Client sees:** `HTTP 502 Bad Gateway` (ALB) or connection resets / TCP RST (NLB). - **Target Group Console displays:** `Target.FailedHealthChecks` or `HealthCheck.Unhealthy`. - **Impact:** Entire availability zones or backend services become unreachable. results.question: How do ephemeral containers troubleshoot a running pod in Kubernetes without restarting it?
results.answer: For a complete list of allowed fields, see the [EphemeralContainer reference documentation](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#ephemeralcontainer-v1-core). Ephemeral containers are created using a special `ephemeralcontainers` handler in the API rather than by adding them directly to `pod.spec`, so it's not possible to add an ephemeral container using `kubectl edit`. Like regular containers, you may not change or remove an ephemeral container after you have added it to a Pod [ephemeral-containers.md#ephemeral-containers.md-c2] Once the {{< glossary_tooltip text="scheduler" term_id="kube-scheduler" >}} assigns a Pod to a Node, the kubelet starts creating containers for that Pod using a {{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}. There are three possible container states: `Waiting`, `Running`, and `Terminated`. To check the state of a Pod's containers, you can use `kubectl describe pod <name-of-pod>`. The output shows the state for each container within that Pod [pod-lifecycle.md#pod-lifecycle.md-c5] {{< note >}} Ephemeral containers are not supported by [static pods](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/). {{< /note >}} [ephemeral-containers.md#ephemeral-containers.md-c2]

results.question: How do you triage high queue execution latency for Sidekiq background jobs in GitLab production?
results.answer: Defer execution of all jobs of that class, using either: - Chatops: ```shell /chatops gitlab run feature set run_sidekiq_jobs_Example::SlowWorker false --ignore-feature-flag-consistency-check --ignore-production-check ``` - Rails console: ```ruby Feature.disable(:"run_sidekiq_jobs_Example::SlowWorker") ``` The above action will cause sidekiq workers to defer (rather than execute) all jobs of that class, including jobs currently waiting in the queue [disabling-a-worker.md#disabling-a-worker.md-c0] Defer execution of all jobs of that class, using either: - Chatops: This should be run in the `#production` ```shell /chatops gitlab run feature set run_sidekiq_jobs_Example::SlowWorker false --ignore-feature-flag-consistency-check --ignore-production-check ``` - On the production rails node run the following to start the rails console: ```shell sudo gitlab-rails console ``` After it starts, run: ```ruby Feature.disable(:"run_sidekiq_jobs_Example::SlowWorker") ``` The action will cause sidekiq workers to defer (rather than execute) all jobs of that class, including jobs currently waiting in the queue [SidekiqQueueTooLarge.md#SidekiqQueueTooLarge.md-c8] The [sidekiq: Worker Detail dashboard](https://dashboards.gitlab.net/d/sidekiq-worker-detail/sidekiq3a-worker-detail) may be helpful in checking a worker's enqueue rate, queue size, and summed execution time spent in shared dependencies like the DB [disabling-a-worker.md#disabling-a-worker.md-c0]

results.question: What actions should be taken when Redis memory usage reaches maxmemory-policy eviction limits?
results.answer: To check memory utilization of redis via cli on a node, run the following: ```shell sudo gitlab-redis-cli info memory ``` Key fields to check: - `used_memory_human` — current memory in use - `maxmemory_human` — the configured limit - `mem_fragmentation_ratio` — values well above `1.5` indicate fragmentation; consider running [`MEMORY PURGE`](https://redis.io/commands/memory-purge/) - `used_memory_rss_human` — RSS as seen by the OS, which includes fragmentation overhead First check the eviction policy, as this determines how to interpret memory pressure: ```shell sudo gitlab-redis-cli config get maxmemory-policy ``` If the policy is `noeviction` (which is the case for `redis-cluster-shared-state`), Redis will **not** evict keys when `maxmemory` is reached — instead, write commands will start failing with `OOM command not allowed`. In this case `evicted_keys` will stay at `0` even under full memory saturation, so it is not a reliable signal [redis-cluster.md#redis-cluster.md-c10] It has the `Memory Saturation`, `Memory Used`, `Redis RSS Usage` and `Memory Fragmentation` panels for every node in the cluster [redis-cluster.md#redis-cluster.md-c10]
